point_one.role: Give listeners a counterintuitive decision rule: household crisper labels are not a universal fruit-versus-vegetable taxonomy, and even manufacturers can classify the same produce differently. The point should turn that ambiguity into a practical, mechanism-based way to judge clear cases rather than merely presenting it as a research limitation.
point_one.new_listener_takeaway: A “Fruit Bin” label or a commercial 90–95% relative-humidity figure for strawberries or oranges cannot automatically be translated into “use the high-humidity drawer” at home. For clearer cases, listeners should focus on whether the food releases substantial ethylene or loses water quickly, rather than relying on its produce category.
point_one.evidence_anchor: FACT-03 v4: the ethylene-versus-water-loss framework; UC Davis’s 90–95% commercial storage figures; and the conflicting GE and Samsung household guidance for strawberries and oranges. FACT-01 and FACT-02 support the distinction between vented, low-humidity storage and moisture-retaining, high-humidity storage.
point_one.why_it_matters: This prevents listeners from treating drawer labels or commercial storage numbers as universal rules and helps them make a more reliable choice when a food does not fit a simple fruit-or-vegetable category.
point_one.must_not_overlap_with_full_story: Do not repeat the basic explanation that low-humidity drawers vent air while high-humidity drawers retain moisture, or re-explain what ethylene does and why leafy greens wilt.
point_one.must_not_overlap_with_other_point: Do not discuss which foods should be kept out of the refrigerator, or the distinction between counter storage and a cool, dry storage place; that is Point Two’s two-stage sorting rule.

point_two.role: Add a pre-check that changes the order of the listener’s decisions: first ask whether the produce belongs in the refrigerator at all, and only then choose a crisper setting. This makes the advice a two-step storage routine rather than a drawer-only trick.
point_two.new_listener_takeaway: A perfectly chosen humidity setting cannot correct the mistake of refrigerating a tomato or banana, which Iowa State identifies as counter-storage items. Potatoes, sweet potatoes, onions, and garlic instead need a cool, dry environment, so they should not be casually treated as identical to counter-stored tomatoes and bananas.
point_two.evidence_anchor: FACT-04 v2: tomatoes and bananas are recommended for counter storage, while potatoes, sweet potatoes, onions, and garlic need a cool, dry environment and do not require refrigeration.
point_two.why_it_matters: It stops listeners from applying the crisper rule mechanically to every item in the produce aisle and prevents the article’s advice from becoming the inaccurate message that all produce belongs in one of the refrigerator drawers.
point_two.must_not_overlap_with_full_story: Do not repeat the low- versus high-humidity mechanics, the ethylene explanation, or the examples of foods that wilt quickly if those are covered in the Full Story.
point_two.must_not_overlap_with_other_point: Do not analyze conflicting manufacturer recommendations, commercial 90–95% humidity figures, or the failure of the fruit-versus-vegetable shortcut; those are Point One’s specific contribution.
